blocks.text: Sometimes an old photograph makes me stop at one face. Who were they? Who kept this picture? I’d like to follow those small questions with you, through Ohio’s libraries, archives, and community collections. We’ll meet different people keeping different memories. There’s room to listen carefully here.

I’d start with a small change of scale. Ohio’s memories sit in state collections, local libraries, tribal archives, family albums, neighborhood groups, and recordings still being made. An archive keeps records; the people caring for them explain where they came from and how they fit together. Let’s notice both, without expecting one collection to speak for everybody.

blocks.title: A statewide archive and a shared portal

blocks.text: Ohio History Connection is one doorway: it runs the State Archives and State Historic Preservation Office, museums and historic sites, and holds manuscripts, photographs, audiovisual records, and oral histories. Ohio Memory brings digital material from OHC and partner institutions together. I’d look for the supplying partner on the item record. The place displaying an image online and the organization holding it can be different.

blocks.title: Read the record in its own terms

steps.title: Who made it?
steps.text: A letter, government file, recording, and museum label come from different makers and purposes.

steps.title: Who describes it?
steps.text: Check the repository or community collection that supplied and cataloged the item.

steps.title: What does it support?
steps.text: Keep narrator, date, interview question, access terms, and limits attached to what you conclude.

blocks.text: An oral history holds a named person’s account, with a recording date and interview context. I find a voice more compelling when those details stay close. Let’s hear what this person chose to tell us without asking them to speak for everyone.
blocks.title: Keep the narrator in view

blocks.text: What sort of thing have we found? A letter keeps what one writer chose to say. A government file shows an institution’s way of recording people and events. An oral history lets us hear a named narrator, with interview questions, date, recording conditions, transcript, and permissions around that voice. A museum label is someone’s interpretation of evidence. I like starting with that simple question before asking a record to tell us more than it can.

Ohio Memory describes oral history as a way to keep individual experience and follow changing communities. OHC’s Gay Ohio History Initiative has gathered accounts from people who shaped LGBTQ+ Ohio life, including organizers and bar owners. The Summit Station project names Petie Brown, CJ Curtis, and Judy Long. I’d stay with the narrator and project when reading an excerpt. Their testimony deserves attention as their own, rather than being made to represent all LGBTQ+ Ohioans.

The partner list can take us somewhere smaller too. Ohio Memory includes GOHI and local institutions such as libraries; photographs, newspapers, school records, and organizational papers may be held regionally. Have family or organization records you’d like to offer? I’d ask the repository what it collects, how access works, and how it keeps the original context with the material.

blocks.title: Credit tribal archives on their own terms

blocks.text: For present-day tribal knowledge, let’s turn to tribal sources. Indigenous objects held by the state can’t take their place. OHC’s American Indian Policy recognizes relationships with tribes in interpretation and collections care; Ohio Memory names the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma as a digital-library partner. I’d follow that collection with the Tribe’s name attached. It shares selected material through that partnership, not a single view belonging to every Shawnee community or Native nation.

Choose one Ohio place you’re curious about. I’d look for an institutional record, a community-held collection, and a first-person account, then compare who made them and what each describes. A street or school may look quite different in each. Before a visit or image reuse, check the repository’s hours, reading-room rules, advance requests, handling requirements, and permissions. A thumbnail doesn’t promise that every page is online.

I’m happy to leave with another question. An archive doesn’t need to give us one tidy Ohio story to be worth our time. Keep names, dates, collection partners, and restrictions with the records; look to living communities’ own organizations for their present-day words. Archivists, families, libraries, cultural organizations, tribal nations, and the people sharing their stories all take part in this continuing work.
A name, a date, someone’s voice. I’m glad we stayed with the story a little longer. Let’s keep those details close. ♡
